title: Smith’s division of labor as a mechanism
prompt: In Wealth of Nations I.i, Smith links specialization to improvements in dexterity, less time switching tasks and machinery. Which constructed observation most directly illustrates the switching-time channel?
correct: Workers produce more with the same tools and hours because they spend fewer minutes changing between operations.
wrong: Workers produce more solely because they work twice as many hours.
Output rises only because the product price rises.
The workforce grows while each worker’s output is unchanged.
explanation: The mechanism concerns time recovered within a fixed workday. It does not require an increase in labor hours, a price change or a larger workforce.
hint: Identify the resource saving associated specifically with moving between tasks.
skill: smith’s division of labor as a mechanism

title: The extent of the market and specialization
prompt: Smith’s Wealth of Nations I.iii argues that the division of labor is limited by the extent of the market. A specialist can efficiently make 100 items daily, but the isolated community buys only 5 and the specialist needs income from other activities. What does opening access to additional buyers change?
correct: It can make sustained specialization viable by expanding outlets for the specialist’s surplus output.
wrong: It proves demand is irrelevant to specialization.
It automatically raises the specialist’s physical productivity to infinity.
It eliminates the need to exchange with other producers.
explanation: A larger outlet supports producing beyond one’s own needs and exchanging for other goods. The argument connects specialization with market reach, not merely with technical capacity.
hint: Ask how a specialist acquires other necessities after producing one narrow product.
skill: the extent of the market and specialization

title: Natural price is not an ethical label
prompt: In Smith’s distinction in Wealth of Nations I.vii, natural price covers ordinary rates of wages, profit and rent, while market price can depart from it. Which reading avoids confusing an analytical category with a moral judgment?
correct: Natural price refers to a benchmark of ordinary remuneration, not automatically the ethically just price.
wrong: Every market price different from natural price is morally forbidden by definition.
Natural price is the price of goods produced without tools.
Market price can never differ from natural price.
explanation: Smith’s classification explains price adjustment around ordinary component returns. The adjective does not by itself supply an ethical test for any transaction.
hint: Read the definition through its cost and remuneration components.
skill: natural price is not an ethical label

title: A market-price deviation and entry
prompt: In a constructed illustration of Smith’s natural-market-price distinction, ordinary remuneration requires a price of 10, but current price is 14. Entry is free, inputs can expand at unchanged costs and demand is fixed. Which adjustment tends to remove the excess return?
correct: Entry expands supply and puts downward pressure on the market price.
wrong: Exit reduces supply until price rises further.
A price above 10 makes all production unprofitable by assumption.
No adjustment is possible because natural price is a legal price ceiling.
explanation: Given expandable supply and ordinary costs, the excess return attracts resources. This illustration holds input costs fixed; it is not a general claim that all industries have horizontal long-run supply.
hint: Follow the incentive created by returns above the stipulated ordinary level.
skill: a market-price deviation and entry

title: Ricardo’s distributional question
prompt: Ricardo’s Principles preface frames political economy around the distribution of output among rent, profits and wages. In a constructed economy with net product 100, rent 20 and wages 50, what residual is assigned to profits if these categories exhaust the net product?
explanation: Under the stated exhaustive accounting, profits are 100−20−50=30. The calculation illustrates a distributional question rather than measuring output growth.
hint: Allocate the net product once across the three stipulated categories.
skill: ricardo’s distributional question

title: Differential rent on two grades of land
prompt: In a simplified Ricardian rent illustration, equal doses of labor and capital cost 60 and yield 100 grain units on good land or 80 on marginal land. Grain sells for 1 per unit, and the marginal land’s residual 20 is the common normal return, with zero rent there. What is good land’s differential rent?
correct: 20 monetary units.
wrong: 40 monetary units.
80 monetary units.
Zero because both plots use equal inputs.
explanation: Good land earns revenue 100, pays input cost 60 and the same normal return 20, leaving rent 20. Equivalently its excess yield over the no-rent margin is 20.
hint: Compare equally costly cultivation with the marginal no-rent alternative.
skill: differential rent on two grades of land

title: Rent as a differential rather than a uniform cost
prompt: In Ricardo’s differential-rent argument, a freely available marginal plot earns no rent while superior land earns a surplus at the same crop price. Why does adding superior land’s rent to every plot’s necessary production cost misrepresent this argument?
correct: The margin can produce without paying rent; superior land’s rent reflects its advantage over that margin.
wrong: Every plot must pay identical rent regardless of fertility.
Zero-rent land cannot produce any crop.
Rent and wages are the same category by definition.
explanation: The no-rent margin matters for the price required to cultivate the least advantageous land in use. Superior land’s differential is not an identical additional outlay required on every plot.
hint: Start from the conditions of production on land that earns no rent.
skill: rent as a differential rather than a uniform cost

title: Relative costs in a trade illustration
prompt: In a constructed labor-only example of Ricardo’s comparative-cost argument, country A needs 2 hours per cloth unit and 4 per wine unit; B needs 6 per cloth and 8 per wine. Labor cannot move internationally. Which comparative advantage follows?
correct: A has comparative advantage in cloth; B in wine.
wrong: A has comparative advantage in both because it uses fewer hours in both.
B has comparative advantage in cloth because it uses more labor there.
Neither can gain from trade because A is absolutely more productive in both.
explanation: A sacrifices 0.5 wine per cloth, compared with B’s 0.75. Cloth is relatively cheaper in A even though A has an absolute productivity advantage in both goods.
hint: Compute opportunity costs within each country before comparing countries.
skill: relative costs in a trade illustration

title: A mutually beneficial barter ratio
prompt: Using a constructed labor-only example, A’s opportunity cost of one cloth is 0.5 wine and B’s is 0.75 wine. Ignore transport and other trade costs. Which proposed exchange ratio lies strictly between the two opportunity costs?
correct: One cloth for 0.6 wine.
wrong: One cloth for 0.4 wine.
One cloth for 0.8 wine.
One cloth for 1 wine.
explanation: At 0.6, A receives more wine per cloth than its internal cost, while B obtains cloth for less wine than its internal cost. This demonstrates a possible mutually beneficial ratio, not its equilibrium determination.
hint: Look for a price strictly inside the opportunity-cost interval.
skill: a mutually beneficial barter ratio

title: Ricardo’s machinery qualification
prompt: In the machinery chapter of the later edition of Principles, Ricardo explicitly considers machinery that can benefit owners while harming laborers. Which conclusion follows about representing his position?
correct: It is inaccurate to attribute to him an unconditional claim that every machinery adoption immediately benefits every class.
wrong: He argued that machinery can never benefit anyone.
He denied that distributional consequences can differ from total gains.
He held that labor displacement is logically impossible.
explanation: The chapter qualifies an earlier view by separating effects on different classes. Recognizing that qualification avoids turning a conditional argument into an unrestricted technological-optimism claim.
hint: Distinguish aggregate or owner gains from the outcome for laborers.
skill: ricardo’s machinery qualification

title: Total usefulness and the final increment
prompt: Jevons distinguishes total utility from the degree of utility of an additional amount. In a constructed example, water provides enormous total benefit but an extra cup adds little benefit at an abundant supply. Which statement respects the distinction?
correct: High total usefulness can coexist with low utility at the margin.
wrong: High total usefulness necessarily makes the final cup the most valuable item available.
Total and marginal utility are identical quantities by definition.
Low marginal utility means water has no total usefulness.
explanation: The contribution of an extra unit depends on how much is already available. It need not equal the total contribution of the entire stock.
hint: Compare the value of the whole quantity with the value of one additional unit.
skill: total usefulness and the final increment

title: Diminishing marginal utility without falling total utility
prompt: A modern mathematical illustration uses U(q)=10q−q² for 0≤q≤5. At q=3, what are marginal utility and the sign of its change as q rises?
correct: Marginal utility is 4 and it is declining.
wrong: Marginal utility is 21 and it is rising.
Marginal utility is −2 and total utility must be falling.
Marginal utility is 4 and it is constant.
explanation: U′(q)=10−2q, so U′(3)=4, while U″(q)=−2. Total utility is still increasing at q=3 although each further increment contributes less. This is an illustration, not Jevons’s numerical example.
hint: Differentiate once for the marginal level and again for its slope.
skill: diminishing marginal utility without falling total utility

title: Past labor and current exchange value
prompt: In Jevons’s exchange discussion, past labor is not an independent determinant of present exchange value merely because it was expended. A useless object took 100 hours to make, cannot be repurposed and gives nobody any benefit. Which inference is unsupported?
correct: That its past labor cost alone guarantees a positive current exchange price.
wrong: That the hours were expended even if buyers do not value the object.
That producing the object could have been a costly mistake.
That current desirability matters to the exchange problem.
explanation: An irrecoverable past cost does not itself create present utility or demand. The point does not deny that production conditions can affect available supplies and thereby value.
hint: Separate sunk effort from the present conditions of exchange.
skill: past labor and current exchange value

title: Equal marginal benefit per unit of expenditure
prompt: A constructed marginal-choice model has an interior optimum with divisible goods. At the current bundle MUx=12 and MUy=8, while px=3 and py=2. What does the marginal-benefit-per-money condition say?
correct: The two ratios are equal at 4, satisfying this necessary interior condition.
wrong: The bundle cannot be optimal because 12 differs from 8.
Spending must move toward x because its total marginal utility is larger.
The goods must have identical prices at an optimum.
explanation: The relevant comparison is MUx/px=12/3 and MUy/py=8/2. Equality is the first-order allocation condition under the stated setup; it is not by itself a global-optimality proof without curvature assumptions.
hint: Normalize each marginal benefit by its price.
skill: equal marginal benefit per unit of expenditure

title: Ordinal representation and measurable intensity
prompt: Two utility representations are U(x,y)=xy and V(x,y)=log(xy), with x,y>0. In the later ordinal interpretation of preferences, what is unchanged by replacing U with V?
correct: The ranking of bundles and the choices implied by that ranking.
wrong: Every numerical marginal utility.
Every difference in utility between two bundles.
A measurement of how many times happier one person is than another.
explanation: Log is strictly increasing, so the two functions represent the same ordering. Their numerical levels and derivatives differ. This is a modern ordinal comparison, not an assertion that Jevons used ordinal utility.
hint: Check whether the transformation preserves every pairwise ordering.
skill: ordinal representation and measurable intensity

title: A boundary choice and the limits of an equality rule
prompt: In a constructed utility model, U(x,y)=2x+y, prices are px=1 and py=1 and income is 10. Goods are divisible and nonnegative. Why is demanding MUx/px=MUy/py at the optimum inappropriate here?
correct: The optimum is a corner at x=10,y=0, so the interior equality condition does not apply.
wrong: No optimum exists because the marginal utilities differ.
The consumer must split expenditure equally to force equal marginal utilities.
Both goods must be consumed because both provide positive utility.
explanation: A unit of spending always produces twice as much utility in x. The nonnegativity boundary prevents the interior equal-ratio condition from being necessary at the optimum.
hint: Check whether an interior solution exists before applying an interior first-order condition.
skill: a boundary choice and the limits of an equality rule

title: Marshall’s other-things-equal method
prompt: Marshall describes isolating a few forces while temporarily holding others inactive, then allowing more interactions into the analysis. What does this method mean?
correct: The excluded forces are provisionally held fixed for analysis, not asserted to be nonexistent.
wrong: Every excluded force is permanently irrelevant in reality.
Economic explanations cannot consider interactions between markets.
A partial model automatically proves all of its predictions at every scale.
explanation: The analytical isolation is a staged simplification. It can be useful while remaining conditional on the forces being held fixed.
hint: Distinguish a temporary analytical restriction from an empirical claim of irrelevance.
skill: marshall’s other-things-equal method

title: Time periods defined by adjustment possibilities
prompt: Marshall emphasizes that short and long periods depend on the problem rather than a universal number of calendar days. In a constructed industry, equipment is fixed over a month but can be expanded over a year. Which distinction is relevant?
correct: The year permits an adjustment margin that is unavailable within the month.
wrong: Every economic long run is exactly one year.
Calendar time has no relation to production choices.
Equipment must be fixed in the long run because it was fixed initially.
explanation: Period distinctions organize which responses have time to occur. Their duration can vary with the technology and decision under study.
hint: Identify the variable allowed to adjust in one horizon but not the other.
skill: time periods defined by adjustment possibilities

title: Demand and supply as joint conditions
prompt: A constructed market has Qd=20−P and Qs=P, both applicable over the chosen adjustment horizon. A commentator says equilibrium price can be derived from demand alone with no supply information. What is the model’s implication?
correct: Both conditions are needed here; solving them jointly gives P=10.
wrong: Demand alone fixes P=20 regardless of supply.
Supply alone fixes P=0 regardless of demand.
Price is not determined even when both equations are supplied.
explanation: Equilibrium equates 20−P with P, yielding 10. In this model neither schedule alone selects the common price. The exercise illustrates a joint determination rather than assigning every historical theory the same equations.
hint: Solve the market-clearing condition using both schedules.
skill: demand and supply as joint conditions

title: Different theories can ask different questions
prompt: One value theory explains ordinary reproducible-good exchange ratios under specified production and distribution conditions. Another asks how a consumer reallocates an extra unit of expenditure among goods. What comparison is most careful?
correct: First align the explanandum and assumptions; the second question is not automatically a refutation of every answer to the first.
wrong: Any marginal-choice result immediately disproves every production-based statement.
Different questions mean the theories can never have conflicting implications.
Both theories must be identical because they use the word value.
explanation: Some disagreements concern the object being explained as well as substantive assumptions. A fair comparison identifies where predictions genuinely overlap before testing their incompatibility.
hint: Specify what each theory is trying to explain before comparing its answer.
skill: different theories can ask different questions

title: Labor-power and the labor performed
prompt: In Capital I, chapter 6, Marx distinguishes labor-power sold by the worker from the labor subsequently performed. Which distinction is central to that argument?
correct: The capacity to work is purchased for a period; using that capacity can create a value different from its own value.
wrong: A wage contract directly sells all future labor for eternity in every case.
Labor-power means only the machines owned by employers.
The value of labor-power is defined as identical to all value created during any working day.
explanation: The distinction separates the commodity purchased from what its use produces. It is a component of Marx’s account, not an assumption that every realized price always equals a labor value.
hint: Distinguish a productive capacity from the result of using it.
skill: labor-power and the labor performed

title: Necessary and surplus labor time
prompt: In a constructed illustration of Marx’s chapter 9 categories, a ten-hour working day contains four hours of necessary labor and six hours of surplus labor. What is the rate of surplus-value s/v in this illustration?
explanation: The rate is surplus labor divided by necessary labor: 6/4=1.5. Dividing surplus time by the entire day would produce a different ratio.
hint: Use necessary labor, not the full day, as the denominator.
skill: necessary and surplus labor time

title: The surplus-value rate is not the profit rate
prompt: In a constructed value-accounting example, constant capital c=60, variable capital v=20 and surplus-value s=20. Define the surplus-value rate as s/v and the profit rate on advanced capital as s/(c+v). What are the two rates?
correct: 100% and 25%, respectively.
wrong: 25% and 100%, respectively.
100% and 100%, respectively.
20% and 20%, respectively.
explanation: The denominators differ: 20/20=1, whereas 20/80=0.25. The illustration uses the stated value categories and is not an empirical reconciliation of values and observed prices.
hint: Write each ratio using its own denominator.
skill: the surplus-value rate is not the profit rate

title: Socially necessary time versus individual slowness
prompt: In Capital I, chapter 1, Marx’s value category uses socially necessary labor time. Two otherwise comparable producers require two and four hours for the same commodity, while prevailing normal conditions require two. Does individual slowness alone double the commodity’s value in this account?
correct: No; individual extra time is not automatically socially necessary time.
wrong: Yes; every hour personally expended necessarily adds the same exchange value.
Yes; the least efficient producer defines normal conditions in every case.
No; the account assigns no role to labor time at all.
explanation: The relevant category refers to prevailing conditions and normal productivity, not whatever time any individual happens to spend. This avoids confusing a social benchmark with a private inefficiency.
hint: Identify whose production conditions define the benchmark.
skill: socially necessary time versus individual slowness

title: Equivalent exchange and the source of surplus
prompt: A reader claims Marx’s account requires employers to purchase labor-power below its value in every case. In the chapter 6 distinction between labor-power and its use, which response is appropriate?
correct: The argument allows labor-power to be bought at its value while its use produces additional value.
wrong: The claim is required because exchange at equivalent values logically prevents any subsequent production.
The claim is required because Marx identifies labor-power’s value with all value produced.
The value of the purchased capacity and the value created during its use are the same concept by definition.
explanation: Marx’s proposed mechanism distinguishes exchange from production and the purchased capacity from the value generated in use. Whether the framework is empirically adequate is separate from correctly stating its internal argument.
hint: Do not equate the value of an input with everything its productive use yields.
skill: equivalent exchange and the source of surplus

title: A conditional effect of capital composition
prompt: Use a constructed accounting model with profit rate r=s/(c+v). Initially c=60, v=20 and s=20. Then c rises to 80 while v and s stay fixed. What follows, and what does not follow?
correct: r falls from 25% to 20%; this does not prove it must fall when s or v also change.
wrong: r rises to 40% because constant capital rose.
r stays 25% because the surplus-value rate is unchanged.
The calculation proves an unconditional downward trend for every economy.
explanation: With s fixed the denominator rises from 80 to 100. The conditional comparative static does not settle a broader dynamic claim when productivity, exploitation or other components change.
hint: Hold exactly the specified quantities fixed and avoid generalizing beyond that comparison.
skill: a conditional effect of capital composition

title: Veblen’s conspicuous consumption
prompt: In The Theory of the Leisure Class, Veblen analyzes consumption as a display of pecuniary standing. Which constructed case most directly illustrates that mechanism?
correct: A buyer values a publicly visible expensive item partly because observers infer high status from it.
wrong: A buyer selects the cheapest invisible input solely to reduce production cost.
A household drinks water privately only to avoid dehydration.
A firm replaces a tool only because its physical output doubles.
explanation: The mechanism concerns social visibility and pecuniary comparison, not the claim that every purchase has a single status motive. Functional and status motives can coexist.
hint: Look for an audience and a comparison of social standing.
skill: veblen’s conspicuous consumption

title: Status competition and aggregate expenditure
prompt: In a constructed status model, two people care only about having a higher display expenditure than the other. Both raise display spending by 5, their ranking is unchanged and spending uses resources with no other benefit. What happens collectively?
correct: Resources are consumed without improving either person’s relative rank.
wrong: Both become strictly higher-ranked than each other.
No resource cost exists because status is relative.
The unchanged ranking proves every unilateral increase was privately irrational.
explanation: A collective escalation can leave positions unchanged while using resources. That does not imply a unilateral deviation is unattractive when the other person’s expenditure is held fixed.
hint: Distinguish a unilateral incentive from a simultaneous increase by everyone.
skill: status competition and aggregate expenditure

title: Institutions as part of preference formation
prompt: A constructed institutional account says repeated social practices help shape what consumers regard as respectable consumption. How does this differ from treating preferences as fixed primitives for a particular choice problem?
correct: It asks how the preferences themselves develop, rather than only how choices respond to constraints given those preferences.
wrong: It makes any analysis of choices logically impossible.
It assumes prices never influence choices.
It says every individual has identical preferences forever.
explanation: The two approaches can operate at different explanatory levels. An account of habit formation is not the same question as conditional optimization with a given ordering.
hint: Identify which objects are being explained and which are being held fixed.
skill: institutions as part of preference formation

title: Legal rules and the set of feasible bargains
prompt: In a constructed institutional comparison, the same production technology operates under two rules: one permits workers to leave freely, while the other enforces costly exit restrictions. Why can contractual outcomes differ even with identical technology?
correct: Rules alter outside options and the set of feasible actions.
wrong: Technology alone uniquely determines every contract regardless of legal rules.
The two rules give workers identical opportunities by definition.
A legal restriction cannot affect bargaining because it is not a physical input.
explanation: Institutional constraints can change bargaining positions without changing engineering possibilities. This is a specified mechanism, not a claim that all institutions have the same effect.
hint: Compare the alternatives available to each party under the two rules.
skill: legal rules and the set of feasible bargains

title: Effective demand and employment
prompt: In General Theory chapter 3, Keynes locates employment where expected sales proceeds and the aggregate supply price are compatible. Which interpretation captures the relevant challenge to an automatic full-employment result?
correct: Expected expenditure can support an employment level below that associated with full employment.
wrong: The physical ability to produce automatically guarantees buyers for every possible output.
Effective demand means every wish for goods regardless of purchasing expenditure.
Keynes’s argument defines unemployment as physically impossible.
explanation: The mechanism concerns employers’ expected proceeds from hiring and producing. It does not equate technical capacity or unsatisfied wants with a sufficient demand for full-employment output.
hint: Ask what level of production entrepreneurs expect to sell profitably.
skill: effective demand and employment

title: Saving-investment identity versus coordination
prompt: In a closed economy without government, realized income is defined as Y=C+I and realized saving as S=Y−C. Why does the resulting identity S=I not prove that desired saving and desired investment are automatically coordinated at full employment?
correct: The identity concerns realized accounting totals, while plans can adjust through income or unintended inventories.
wrong: An accounting identity permits realized S and I to differ under these definitions.
The identity fixes full-employment income by itself.
Saving is identically zero whenever investment is positive.
explanation: Substitution establishes an ex post equality. It does not supply behavioral equations or an adjustment process that selects full employment. The distinction is central to interpreting Keynes’s discussion of saving and investment.
hint: Separate definitions of realized magnitudes from decisions made before outcomes occur.
skill: saving-investment identity versus coordination

title: A thrift experiment in a demand-led model
prompt: A constructed fixed-price economy has Y=C+I, C=a+0.8Y and I=20 fixed. Autonomous consumption a falls from 20 to 10, and capacity remains slack. What happens to equilibrium income and realized saving?
correct: Income falls from 200 to 150, while saving remains 20.
wrong: Income remains 200 and saving rises to 30.
Income falls by only 10 and saving rises by 10.
Income rises to 250 because thrift necessarily expands current demand.
explanation: Equilibrium gives Y=(a+20)/0.2. Realized saving equals fixed investment 20 in either equilibrium. This conditional result illustrates a thrift paradox rather than claiming that all saving is harmful in every model.
hint: Solve the income equation at both consumption intercepts, then use S=Y−C.
skill: a thrift experiment in a demand-led model

title: Expected capital returns and investment
prompt: In General Theory chapter 11, the marginal efficiency of capital depends on prospective returns relative to supply price. A constructed project costs 100 now and is expected to return 110 next year with no later payoff. If that expected payoff falls to 102, what happens to its break-even discount rate?
correct: It falls from 10% to 2%.
wrong: It rises from 10% to 20%.
It remains 10% because the purchase cost is unchanged.
It becomes 102%.
explanation: The rate solving 100=payoff/(1+r) is r=payoff/100−1. Lower expected proceeds reduce the inducement to invest at any unchanged market interest rate.
hint: Equate supply price with the discounted prospective return.
skill: expected capital returns and investment

title: Liquidity preference as a portfolio question
prompt: In General Theory chapter 13, Keynes distinguishes the decision to save from the choice of how to hold accumulated purchasing power. Which case shows why those are different decisions?
correct: Two households save the same amount but one holds cash and the other bonds.
wrong: Every act of saving uniquely determines a bond purchase.
A household cannot hold money unless it consumes its entire income.
The amount saved determines every future market interest rate without reference to asset demand.
explanation: An income-consumption decision does not uniquely allocate wealth among liquid and interest-bearing assets. The distinction supplies the setting for liquidity preference in the chapter.
hint: Separate the quantity of wealth carried forward from its asset composition.
skill: liquidity preference as a portfolio question

title: An illustrative liquidity-preference schedule
prompt: A constructed liquidity-preference model has real money supply 80 and demand L(r)=100−10r, where r is measured in percentage points and income is fixed. What interest rate clears this asset market?
explanation: Setting 80=100−10r gives r=2 percentage points. This schematic schedule illustrates asset-market clearing and is not presented as Keynes’s estimated equation.
hint: Equate the fixed money stock with desired holdings and retain the rate units.
skill: an illustrative liquidity-preference schedule

title: Confidence and a conditional investment calculation
prompt: Keynes’s chapter 12 discusses the state of confidence surrounding long-term expectations. In a constructed illustration, two investors report the same central forecast but one regards its evidential basis as far less dependable. What should a comparison of their investment decisions avoid assuming?
correct: That the identical central forecast captures every relevant aspect of their expectations.
wrong: That their stated central forecasts are equal.
That confidence concerns the basis for relying on a forecast.
That forecasts can be revised when their supporting evidence changes.
explanation: A single forecast number need not summarize confidence in the evidence behind it. The question concerns that distinction, not a claim that confidence has one universally specified probability formula.
hint: Distinguish the forecast’s central value from confidence in the judgment supporting it.
skill: confidence and a conditional investment calculation

title: A wage cut at the firm and economy levels
prompt: In General Theory chapter 19, Keynes examines several channels through which money-wage changes can affect employment. Why is the partial-equilibrium argument that one firm can sell more by cutting its wage cost insufficient by itself to establish that an economy-wide wage cut restores full employment?
correct: An economy-wide change can also alter demand, prices, debts and expectations, so the individual firm’s unchanged-demand comparison need not carry over.
wrong: Every nominal wage cut necessarily raises every real wage.
The same firm-level sales gain can be added across all firms while total demand is held fixed without checking consistency.
Money wages are absent from all employment decisions by definition.
explanation: The aggregate question changes conditions held fixed in the single-firm comparison. The chapter’s analysis cannot be reduced to a claim that one isolated cost effect always determines total employment.
hint: Identify which supposedly fixed conditions move when all firms and households are affected.
skill: a wage cut at the firm and economy levels

title: A textbook interpretation and its limits
prompt: A later textbook model summarizes goods and money markets using two static schedules at a fixed price level. What is the careful relationship between this construction and the much broader arguments of a primary text such as the General Theory?
correct: It is an interpretation with explicit simplifying assumptions; conclusions outside those assumptions require further argument.
wrong: It must contain every claim in the original text because it uses two markets.
Any feature omitted by the diagram was denied by the original author.
A simplified interpretation can never be analytically useful.
explanation: A formal reconstruction selects mechanisms and imposes closure conditions. It can clarify a question without being an exhaustive transcription of the original work.
hint: Compare the model’s maintained assumptions and omitted mechanisms with its intended purpose.
skill: a textbook interpretation and its limits

title: Why the thrift result is conditional
prompt: Compare two constructed models after households desire less current consumption. Model A has fixed investment and slack capacity; model B has fixed full-employment output and an adjustment mechanism that raises investment by the consumption decline. What differs?
correct: Model A can contract income, while model B reallocates fixed output toward investment.
wrong: Both models must predict the same income contraction because the preference change has the same label.
Model B violates accounting merely because investment rises.
Model A necessarily raises investment because output is below capacity.
explanation: The accounting can hold in both models while the closure and adjustment mechanisms differ. The debate is not resolved by the word saving alone.
hint: Track which variable is allowed to adjust in each model.
skill: why the thrift result is conditional

title: Existence is not a theory of adjustment
prompt: A constructed general-equilibrium argument proves that at least one price vector clears every market. It specifies no out-of-equilibrium price adjustment rule. What does the existence result not establish?
correct: That actual price dynamics converge to an equilibrium.
wrong: That a market-clearing price vector exists under the argument’s assumptions.
That the proof concerns simultaneous compatibility of market choices.
That the argument has maintained assumptions.
explanation: An equilibrium’s existence is logically separate from its stability under a specified dynamic process. A stability claim requires an adjustment rule and additional analysis.
hint: Separate a solution to equilibrium conditions from a path toward that solution.
skill: existence is not a theory of adjustment

title: A numeraire and relative prices
prompt: A two-good exchange model has equilibrium prices (2,4), and all demands are homogeneous of degree zero in prices and nominal wealth. Which proportional price vector represents the same relative prices when wealth is scaled likewise?
explanation: Scaling both prices and nominal wealth by one half leaves budget sets in real terms unchanged. The normalization fixes units of account, not the relative price between goods.
hint: Apply the same scale factor to every nominal magnitude.
skill: a numeraire and relative prices

title: A market implication of the value budget identity
prompt: In a constructed two-good exchange economy, aggregate excess demands obey p₁z₁+p₂z₂=0 at every positive price vector. If market 1 clears and p₂>0, what follows?
correct: Market 2 also clears.
wrong: Market 2 must have positive excess demand.
Market 2 can have arbitrary excess demand despite the identity.
Both goods must have identical prices.
explanation: With z₁=0, the identity becomes p₂z₂=0. The positive second price implies z₂=0. The result depends on the stated aggregate budget identity.
hint: Substitute market clearing into the value identity before dividing by price.
skill: a market implication of the value budget identity

title: Pareto improvement and a distributional tradeoff
prompt: A constructed policy changes two people’s utilities from (4,4) to (7,3). Is it a Pareto improvement according to the criterion that nobody is worse off and someone is better off?
correct: No, because the second person is worse off.
wrong: Yes, because the utility numbers sum to a larger total.
Yes, because one person gains more numerically than the other loses.
The Pareto criterion requires equal utilities, so neither allocation can be assessed.
explanation: The criterion does not aggregate utility gains against another person’s loss. A separate social judgment might favor the change, but it would use information or values beyond the Pareto test.
hint: Check each person’s direction of change rather than adding utility numbers.
skill: pareto improvement and a distributional tradeoff

title: Potential compensation is not actual compensation
prompt: Two people have quasilinear utility in money. A constructed project gives one person a monetary-equivalent gain of 100 and the other a loss of 60. Costless monetary transfers are feasible, but none are made. What does the possibility of compensating the loser establish?
correct: Compensation could leave both people better off, but the uncompensated outcome still harms the losing person.
wrong: The loser has already been compensated by the existence of the gain.
The uncompensated change is a Pareto improvement by definition.
No transfer can improve both people because the gains and losses differ.
explanation: The gain exceeds the loss, leaving room for a transfer between 60 and 100. A feasible compensation test is different from an implemented distributional outcome.
hint: Distinguish an available transfer from a transfer that actually occurs.
skill: potential compensation is not actual compensation

title: Utility scales and interpersonal sums
prompt: Two people’s ordinal utilities at allocation A are (3,1), and at B are (2,3). A researcher sums them and chooses B. If person 1’s utility is rescaled by a positive factor of 10, what happens to that sum ranking?
correct: It reverses, although neither person’s own ranking changes.
wrong: It stays fixed because ordinal utility fixes interpersonal comparisons.
Both people reverse their individual preferences.
The rescaling is inadmissible for any ordinal representation.
explanation: Original sums are 4 and 5. After rescaling person 1, they are 31 and 23. An unweighted sum is not ordinally invariant across independently scaled persons.
hint: Recompute the sums after a transformation that preserves each individual ordering.
skill: utility scales and interpersonal sums

title: Social weights as an explicit judgment
prompt: A constructed welfare criterion is W=αu₁+(1−α)u₂. Allocation A gives utilities (8,2), while B gives (4,6). For which α is A strictly preferred?
wrong: Every α between 0 and 1.
Only α=0.5.
explanation: W(A)−W(B)=4α−4(1−α)=8α−4, which is positive above one half. The ranking depends on an explicitly supplied weighting judgment.
hint: Compute the welfare difference before solving for the weight.
skill: social weights as an explicit judgment

title: A welfare theorem and an omitted external effect
prompt: An analyst invokes a competitive-efficiency result whose maintained assumptions include no unpriced external effects. The actual model under review has an unpriced pollution damage. What is the logically warranted response?
correct: That theorem cannot establish efficiency for this model without addressing the violated assumption.
wrong: Every competitive outcome in the actual model is proven efficient anyway.
The existence of pollution proves no equilibrium can exist.
A failed assumption proves every possible policy intervention improves welfare.
explanation: A theorem’s implication is conditional. Losing a sufficient condition removes this proof; it neither proves nonexistence nor validates every alternative policy.
hint: Separate the absence of a theorem’s guarantee from a universal claim about remedies.
skill: a welfare theorem and an omitted external effect

title: Nonconvex production and marginal-cost pricing
prompt: A constructed firm produces positive output at cost C(q)=10+2q and has no cost if closed. At q=5, price equal to marginal cost is 2. What issue does this create for a simple marginal-cost-pricing decentralization?
correct: Revenue 10 is below total cost 20, so the price does not cover the fixed cost.
wrong: Revenue is 20 and exactly covers cost.
Marginal cost rises to 4 because average cost is 4.
Fixed cost disappears whenever marginal cost is charged.
explanation: At the specified output, p q=2×5=10 while C(5)=20. A rule that equates price to marginal cost does not by itself finance the fixed cost in this nonconvex example.
hint: Compare total revenue with total cost rather than marginal values alone.
skill: nonconvex production and marginal-cost pricing

title: Reconstruction versus textual attribution
prompt: A historian rewrites an early economist’s verbal argument as a modern optimization model with differentiable utility and complete markets. Those assumptions are not documented in the text. What is the defensible description of the exercise?
correct: An interpretive reconstruction whose additional assumptions should be distinguished from the author’s own statements.
wrong: A verbatim statement of the original author’s model.
Proof that the author explicitly accepted every modern assumption.
A useless exercise solely because it uses modern notation.
explanation: Formal reconstruction can expose implications, but added structure must be labeled. Analytical usefulness does not establish historical attribution.
hint: Track which premises come from the source and which the interpreter supplied.
skill: reconstruction versus textual attribution

title: Hayek’s dispersed knowledge problem
prompt: In The Use of Knowledge in Society, Hayek distinguishes general scientific knowledge from knowledge of particular circumstances of time and place. Which constructed example best illustrates the latter?
correct: A workshop manager knows that an otherwise idle local machine is available this afternoon.
wrong: Every observer knows the same abstract production formula.
An optimization exercise assumes all resource information is already assembled in one place.
A national accounting identity defines saving after the fact.
explanation: The example concerns timely, local knowledge that need not be contained in a general scientific rule. The argument asks how such dispersed knowledge can enter coordinated decisions.
hint: Look for useful information specific to a place and moment.
skill: hayek’s dispersed knowledge problem

title: A price signal without the full story
prompt: In Hayek’s tin example, users may economize on tin after its relative price rises without knowing whether the original cause was lost supply or new demand elsewhere. What role does the price play in that argument?
correct: It communicates a changed relative scarcity relevant to users’ adjustments without conveying every underlying event.
wrong: It reveals every causal detail of the original shock.
It proves that every observed price is always socially optimal under every market institution.
It makes users’ local knowledge unnecessary.
explanation: The argument concerns economizing on information needed to adjust resource use. It is not a theorem that all prices under all frictions perfectly measure social costs.
hint: Distinguish information sufficient for an adjustment from complete knowledge of its cause.
skill: a price signal without the full story

title: Friedman’s proposed test of a hypothesis
prompt: In The Methodology of Positive Economics, Friedman emphasizes comparing a hypothesis’s implications with experience. Which evaluation is closest to that proposed criterion?
correct: Ask whether the model yields sufficiently accurate implications for its intended domain compared with alternatives.
wrong: Accept a model because its assumptions are maximally detailed, regardless of its implications.
Accept a model because an eminent author wrote it.
Treat a single successful observation as a deductive proof that the model is true.
explanation: The essay prioritizes empirical performance for the purpose at hand and does not treat factual evidence as deductive proof. This states the proposed criterion rather than claiming it settles all methodological disputes.
hint: Evaluate implications and the intended task, not authority or descriptive detail alone.
skill: friedman’s proposed test of a hypothesis

title: Unrealistic assumptions and a criticism’s target
prompt: A model predicts a market outcome accurately in one environment but assumes away a mechanism central to a proposed new policy. In a methodological debate about prediction and assumptions, what should the policy evaluation investigate?
correct: Whether the omitted mechanism changes the model’s implications under that policy.
wrong: The model is guaranteed valid for the policy because it fit the old environment.
Any simplified assumption makes all of the model’s predictions worthless.
Adding every detail, however irrelevant, guarantees a better policy forecast.
explanation: An assumption can be tolerable for one task and consequential for another. The comparison requires evidence or argument about the target intervention, not an unconditional defense or rejection of simplification.
hint: Ask whether the simplification is relevant to the new use of the model.
skill: unrealistic assumptions and a criticism’s target

title: Rational expectations do not mean perfect foresight
prompt: A constructed model assumes agents’ forecasts equal the conditional expectation implied by the model and their available information. A later shock is not in that information. Which outcome is compatible with the assumption?
correct: A realized forecast error caused by the unanticipated shock.
wrong: Every realized forecast must equal the outcome exactly.
Agents must know all future shocks before they occur.
The forecast must ignore information available at the time it is formed.
explanation: A conditional mean forecast can be wrong ex post without being systematically wrong relative to the stipulated information. Rational expectations and omniscience are distinct assumptions.
hint: Separate the information set from the realized future state.
skill: rational expectations do not mean perfect foresight

title: A policy rule changes an observed coefficient
prompt: In a constructed model, y=2x+u and policy sets x=b u with b>0 and Var(u)>0. A regression with an intercept of y on x therefore has population slope 2+1/b. If the policy rule changes b from 1 to 2 while the structural equation stays fixed, what happens to that slope?
correct: It falls from 3 to 2.5.
wrong: It stays 2 because every regression coefficient is structural.
It rises from 3 to 4.
The change proves the structural coefficient 2 has changed.
explanation: The policy rule changes the relationship between x and u, so the observed slope changes despite fixed structural coefficient 2. This is an original illustration of regime dependence, not a quotation of a particular author’s model.
hint: Substitute each policy-rule parameter into the reduced-form slope.
skill: a policy rule changes an observed coefficient

title: An accounting equation and a monetary theory
prompt: Define velocity V=PY/M, so MV=PY is an identity. A commentator infers that a 10% rise in M causes exactly a 10% rise in P. Which additional restriction is sufficient for that proportional price change algebraically, while leaving causal assumptions to be justified?
correct: That V and real output Y remain unchanged in the relevant comparison.
wrong: No restriction, because the identity alone fixes every variable’s response.
That Y always rises exactly with M.
That velocity is undefined whenever money is positive.
explanation: An identity constrains jointly realized quantities but does not specify which variables adjust to a policy. Fixing V and Y yields proportional P algebraically; interpreting an intervention still requires a behavioral account.
hint: Identify the variables implicitly held fixed when solving the identity for price.
skill: an accounting equation and a monetary theory

title: Aggregation and a representative response
prompt: A constructed model has each household’s spending equal to the square of its wealth. Economy A has two households with wealth 1 and 3; economy B has wealth 2 and 2. Both have mean wealth 2. Can a response based only on mean wealth reproduce both aggregate spending levels?
correct: No; aggregate spending is 10 in A and 8 in B despite the same mean.
wrong: Yes; both aggregates must equal 8 because the mean is 2.
Yes; both aggregates must equal 10 because there are two households.
No; their mean wealth is different.
explanation: Nonlinearity makes the wealth distribution matter: 1²+3²=10 whereas 2²+2²=8. A representative response requires aggregation conditions beyond matching a mean.
hint: Apply the individual rule before summing, then compare with applying it to the mean.
skill: aggregation and a representative response

title: Calibration targets and independent evidence
prompt: A model’s parameters are chosen specifically to reproduce two empirical moments. It matches those two moments exactly. What does that match alone establish?
correct: Success at reproducing the selected targets, not an independent validation of untested mechanisms or predictions.
wrong: Every mechanism in the model has been separately identified.
All out-of-sample policy predictions are now verified.
The fit is impossible because calibrated models cannot match data.
explanation: Using a fact to select parameters and then citing the same match does not create new evidence. Distinct moments or other independent implications can provide further evaluation.
hint: Distinguish data used to construct the model from evidence used to challenge it.
skill: calibration targets and independent evidence

title: Predictive agreement and welfare disagreement
prompt: Two constructed models predict the same observed quantities over the available sample. They use different unobserved welfare-relevant distortions and rank a new policy oppositely. What is the warranted methodological conclusion?
correct: The observed predictive agreement does not by itself determine the welfare ranking.
wrong: The models must agree on welfare because quantities match.
The more complicated model must have the correct welfare ranking.
Averaging the two welfare rankings makes the result identified.
explanation: Agreement on the observed targets can coexist with disagreement about counterfactual or normative objects. Resolving the policy comparison requires additional evidence or explicit maintained assumptions about the relevant structure.
hint: Ask which parts of the policy objective the observed predictions actually constrain.
skill: predictive agreement and welfare disagreement
